title: Materialized views and data cubes
goal: By the end you can say when a stored query result beats running the query again, what REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW costs with and without CONCURRENTLY, maintain count, sum, average and minimum incrementally under inserts and deletes and explain why MIN, joins and big batches are the hard cases, read a data cube as a stored GROUP BY CUBE, and place pg_ivm, Snowflake, Databricks and streaming databases on that map.

warmup.q: A materialized view keeps, per merchant, `count(*)`, `sum(amount)` and `min(amount)` of its payments. One payment is deleted. Which of the three can the view correct without reading the payments table?
options: All three: subtract the payment from each
Count and sum always; min too, unless the deleted payment was the merchant's minimum
None of them: any delete forces a full refresh
Only count
warmup.why: Count goes down by one and sum by the amount, using only the deleted row. The minimum stays as it is when the deleted amount was larger. But if the deleted payment was the minimum, the view no longer knows the next smallest amount: it was never stored. Then it must read the merchant's remaining payments, or keep more state. "All three" is tempting because subtraction works for the first two; you can't subtract from a minimum. A full refresh is always correct, and it is the expensive way this lesson sets out to avoid.

sections.h: A materialized view stores the answer to a query you keep asking
sections.body:
The settlement dashboard shows each merchant its payments per day: how many and how much. Every merchant who opens it runs the same aggregate. In the Try it, that query reads all 7,356 pages of a 1,000,000-row payments table to return 12 rows for one merchant, about 25 ms. Lesson 7's index on `merchant_id` would cut the pages, but the database still recounts the same payments every time someone looks. With 2,000 merchants reloading the page all day, it computes the same answers over and over.

Version 1 is to do nothing: run the query each time. It's always right, and its cost grows with the table, not with the answer.

Version 2 stores the answer. A job runs the aggregate every few minutes and writes the result into a summary table, `daily_totals`, one row per merchant and day. The dashboard reads 12 rows through an index. Teams have built this by hand for decades: a cron job, a `TRUNCATE`, an `INSERT ... SELECT`.

PostgreSQL has it built in. `CREATE MATERIALIZED VIEW daily_totals AS SELECT ...` runs the query once and stores the rows in a real table that you can index and query like any other. `REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW daily_totals` runs the query again and replaces the contents. In the Try it, building it took about a quarter of a second and produced 24,000 rows, and the dashboard's question then read 14 pages in well under a millisecond. A plain view (`CREATE VIEW`) is different: it stores nothing, and PostgreSQL pastes its query into every statement that uses it.

**A materialized view is a stored query result plus a rule for keeping it right when its inputs change.** That's the picture for this lesson. It is the same deal as an index from lesson 7: a derived copy that makes one kind of read cheap and costs work whenever the data changes. An index copies rows in another order; a materialized view copies the result of a computation.

The rule is where the trouble lives. The stored rows are a snapshot. Insert a payment for merchant 42 and the view still shows 43 payments for that day, not 44: it is stale until the next refresh, and nothing tells the reader. The rest of the lesson is about that rule: when to recompute, what recomputing costs, and how to change only what a new row changes.

try.title: Store the dashboard's answer, then watch it go stale
steps: From `labs/`, start PostgreSQL with `docker compose -f env/postgres.yml up -d --wait` and open psql with `docker compose -f env/postgres.yml exec db psql -U sfz`. The first statement drops `payments` if an earlier lesson left one; the next Try its use this table and view.
Create 1,000,000 payments over 2,000 merchants and 12 days (a few seconds), then run the dashboard's question against the table. Predict the pages it reads.
Create the materialized view and run the same question against it. Then insert one payment for merchant 42 and predict what the view says before and after the refresh.

sections.h: REFRESH recomputes everything, and CONCURRENTLY only changes who waits
sections.body:
A refresh costs the whole query, every time. In the first Try it, one new payment made `REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW daily_totals` read all 1,000,001 payments and rewrite all 24,000 view rows: about a quarter of a second to change one number. The cost follows the size of the inputs, not the size of the change. Refresh every minute and the database recomputes the same 99.99% of the answer 1,440 times a day. Refresh once a night and the dashboard is up to a day stale.

A refresh also locks the view. A plain REFRESH builds the new contents in a new file and swaps it in, holding an `ACCESS EXCLUSIVE` lock on the view while it runs: the strongest lock PostgreSQL has, which makes every `SELECT` on the view wait. On a view that takes 20 minutes to compute, the dashboard hangs for 20 minutes.

`REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW CONCURRENTLY` keeps readers going. It computes the full new result into a temporary table, compares it with the current contents row by row, and applies only the differences as inserts, updates and deletes, under an `EXCLUSIVE` lock that still lets `SELECT` run. To match old rows with new ones it needs a unique index on the view, on plain columns and covering every row; without one PostgreSQL refuses.

It does more work, not less. It still runs the whole query, then the comparison. In the Try it, with one payment changed, the plain refresh took about 0.26 seconds and the concurrent one 0.37. PostgreSQL's documentation puts it carefully: a plain refresh that changes many rows tends to use fewer resources and finish sooner, and CONCURRENTLY may be faster when few rows change. Here, with one row changed, it wasn't. What CONCURRENTLY buys is readers who never wait, and it charges extra work for them.

So recompute-and-replace hits two walls. **Staleness**: the view is only as fresh as the last refresh. And cost: every refresh pays for all the data, however little changed. Refreshing more often trades one wall for the other. Getting past both needs a refresh whose work follows the change.

try.title: Two refreshes, two locks
steps: In the same psql session, ask for a concurrent refresh before the view has a unique index. Predict the error, then create the index.
Run each kind of refresh inside a transaction and read `pg_locks` before rolling back. Predict which lock mode each one holds on the view.
Change one payment and time both refreshes. Predict which is faster.

The plain refresh holds `AccessExclusiveLock` on the view, which blocks every reader until it commits. The concurrent one holds `ExclusiveLock`, which readers' `AccessShareLock` doesn't conflict with, plus `RowExclusiveLock` for the rows it changes. With one payment changed, both reran the whole aggregate, and the concurrent one took longer because it then compared 24,000 old rows with 24,000 new ones. Your times will differ; the order usually won't.

sections.h: Incremental maintenance applies each change as a delta
sections.body:
Version 3 refreshes by the change instead of by the data. Take a view with, per merchant, the count, sum and minimum of its payments. When a payment is inserted, its merchant's row changes in a way you can compute from that payment alone: count plus 1, sum plus the amount, minimum the smaller of the old minimum and the amount. No other view row changes, and nothing in the table has to be read. That rule is a **delta rule**: how a change to the input turns into a change to the output. Incremental view maintenance (IVM) means having a delta rule for every operator in the view's query. The stepper applies four changes to a small view.

Deletes mirror inserts for count and sum: minus 1, minus the amount, and when a merchant's count reaches 0 its row leaves the view. Average has no delta rule of its own, because you can't take one payment back out of an average. So a maintained view stores sum and count and divides when someone reads it, for the same reason lesson 8 kept sums and counts in its time buckets.

MIN and MAX break the pattern. Inserts are easy: compare. Deleting anything above the minimum is easy: the minimum stays. Delete the payment that was the minimum, and the view can't know the next smallest amount, because it never stored it. There are two ways out. Read the merchant's remaining payments again, which needs an index on the merchant and costs one group's rows; or keep more state, every amount with how many rows have it, sorted, per group, which costs memory for every row. pg_ivm takes the first way. Streaming engines take the second.

Joins are harder still. In a view over `payments JOIN merchants`, a new payment must be joined with its merchant, so the delta rule reads the other table and needs an index there. One renamed merchant changes every view row built from that merchant's payments, possibly millions. When both tables change in one transaction, the delta has three parts: new payments with old merchants, old payments with new merchants, and new with new. Miss the third, or count a pair in two parts, and the view drifts from the truth without an error.

And deltas aren't always cheaper. In the Try it, 1,000 changes to 20,000 payments cost 1,402 rows of work incrementally, against 20 million for a full recompute after each change. But a batch that deleted 90% of the table cost 35,994 rows as deltas, most of it rescanning merchants whose minimum had just been deleted, against 2,200 for one recompute at the end. Deltas win when changes are few; big batches are cheaper to recompute.

try.title: Count the work: deltas against recomputing
steps: Read `ViewDemo.kt`. It loads 20,000 payments over 200 merchants into the lab's `PaymentTable`, then applies 1,000 random inserts and deletes two ways: through the reference `IncrementalView`, and by a full recompute after every change. Then it deletes 90% of the table in one batch. It counts rows touched, not time, so your numbers will match.
Before you run it from `labs/` (no Docker needed), predict the ratio of rows touched for the 1,000 changes, and which strategy wins the batch.
try.expect:
```text
base table: 20,000 payments over 200 merchants
1,000 changes: 500 inserts, 500 deletes, 4 of them removed a merchant's minimum

strategy                            base rows read  view rows written
full recompute after every change       20,000,500            200,000
incremental (delta rules)                      402              1,000
incremental touched 1,402 rows: 0.007% of the recompute's 20,200,500

a batch deleting 18,000 payments (90% of the table):
  incremental, one delta per change: 35,994 rows touched (498 min rescans)
  one full recompute afterwards:     2,200 rows touched
```

For the stream of changes, every change wrote one view row and only 4 deletes read anything, about 100 rows each, the merchant whose minimum went. Recomputing after every change read the whole table 1,000 times. The batch turns it around: as a merchant's payments are deleted in random order, its minimum keeps disappearing, so the view rescanned merchants 498 times, while one recompute afterwards read the 2,000 surviving rows once. The first run compiles the demo, which takes longer.

sections.h: A data cube stores every grouping, and answers nothing else
sections.body:
Some dashboards ask one aggregate along many dimensions: totals by day, by currency, by merchant category, by any two of them, by all three, and the grand total. One materialized view per combination would work. A **data cube** stores them all at once.

Picture payments summed by day and currency as a grid: one cell per (day, currency) holding the total. Add a total per currency at the bottom (all days), a total per day at the right (all currencies), and the grand total in the corner. That grid with its margins, in the figure, is a two-dimensional cube. Add a third dimension, merchant category, and it becomes a block of cells with totals along every face, edge and corner. A question that groups by some of the dimensions and filters on their values is one cell, or the sum of a few.

You've written the SQL for it already. `GROUP BY CUBE (day, currency, category)` from the SQL track's aggregation lesson produces every grouping set of the three columns: 2 x 2 x 2 = 8 of them, from (day, currency, category) down to (), the grand total. Store that result in a materialized view and you have a data cube. Add `GROUPING(day, currency, category)`, a bitmask that says which columns were rolled up, because a rolled-up column shows as NULL and would otherwise look like a real NULL. In the Try it, 12 days x 4 currencies x 5 categories give 240 base cells, and CUBE adds 150 total cells: 390 rows answer every grouped question about the million payments.

The price is size and rigidity. Cells multiply: 365 days, 2,000 merchants and 4 currencies give up to 2.9 million base cells, and each extra dimension multiplies again, which is why cubes use a few dimensions with few values each. And a cube answers only questions about its dimensions. "What share of the money came from payments over 500 euros?" needs each payment's amount, which no cell kept; the cube summed it away. That's why warehouses keep the raw rows and use cubes, like materialized views in general, as accelerators in front of them. The Batch track's lesson on warehouses and dimensional models builds the star schemas cubes are cut from.

Keeping a cube fresh means maintaining all its grouping sets at once. One new payment changes one cell at every level, 8 cells for three dimensions: COUNT and SUM cells take the deltas of the last section, and MIN cells bring back its delete problem.

try.title: Build a cube from the payments and read it
steps: In the same psql session, store `GROUP BY CUBE` over day, currency and a category derived from the merchant id. Before you count, predict how many rows each level of the cube has, and in total.
Answer three questions from the cube, then check one against the table. When you are done with this lesson, stop and delete the database: `docker compose -f env/postgres.yml down -v`.

code.title: psql
code.src:
-- 1. a cube over three dimensions: day, currency and the merchant's category
CREATE MATERIALIZED VIEW sales_cube AS
SELECT (created_at AT TIME ZONE 'UTC')::date AS day, currency,
       (ARRAY['grocery','travel','fuel','online','retail'])[1 + merchant_id % 5] AS category,
       GROUPING((created_at AT TIME ZONE 'UTC')::date, currency,
                (ARRAY['grocery','travel','fuel','online','retail'])[1 + merchant_id % 5]) AS g,
       count(*) AS n, sum(amount_cents) AS sum_cents
FROM payments
GROUP BY CUBE (1, 2, 3);

-- 2. cells per level (g is a bitmask: 4 = day rolled up, 2 = currency, 1 = category)
SELECT g, count(*) AS cells FROM sales_cube GROUP BY g ORDER BY g;

-- 3. three questions, each one or a few rows of the cube
SELECT sum_cents FROM sales_cube WHERE g = 7;                                   -- grand total
SELECT currency, sum_cents FROM sales_cube WHERE g = 5 ORDER BY currency;       -- per currency, all days
SELECT n, sum_cents FROM sales_cube WHERE g = 2 AND day = '2026-10-05' AND category = 'travel';

-- 4. check one of them against the table
SELECT sum(amount_cents) FROM payments WHERE currency = 'SEK';

sections.body:
Every product makes the same three choices: when it applies deltas, which queries it can maintain, and what it does with the rest.

PostgreSQL itself only recomputes, with or without CONCURRENTLY. The pg_ivm extension (1.17, October 2026, for PostgreSQL 13 to 19) adds incrementally maintainable materialized views, made with `pgivm.create_immv('name', 'SELECT ...')`. It maintains them immediately: triggers on the base tables apply the deltas in the same transaction as the change, so the view is never stale, and every write to the base table pays for it. It handles inner and outer joins, DISTINCT, and count, sum, avg, min and max; when a deleted row held a group's min or max, it recomputes that group from the base tables, as your lab does. Window functions, HAVING, ORDER BY and UNION are among what it can't maintain. Its README measures the trade on pgbench data: a single-row UPDATE took about 9 ms next to an ordinary materialized view and 15 ms with a view that kept itself current, while REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW took 20 seconds.

Cloud warehouses maintain views on a schedule. A Snowflake dynamic table is a query plus a target lag, how far behind its sources it may fall. It refreshes in one of four modes: INCREMENTAL merges only the changes since the last refresh, FULL reruns the query, ADAPTIVE goes incremental but rebuilds when an incremental refresh would cost much more, and AUTO picks INCREMENTAL or FULL once, at creation, and never looks again. Snowflake's docs warn that when a large share of the data changes between refreshes, incremental can be slower than full, the crossover of the lab's batch. EXCEPT, INTERSECT and exact percentiles can't be refreshed incrementally. Databricks materialized views refresh incrementally only on serverless compute; a cost analysis picks incremental or full for each refresh, and anything it can't make incremental is fully recomputed.

Streaming databases make IVM the whole product. Materialize and RisingWave read changes continuously, from Kafka topics or a database's change stream, and keep every view current as they arrive. Materialize serves results from memory in an index or persists them to durable storage; RisingWave keeps them in Hummock, an LSM tree on object storage, lesson 5's design again. They pay in state: to maintain a MIN under deletes or a join, they keep the second way out from the delta section, and that state grows with the data. The Stream processing track builds this machinery, and the Derived data track's lesson on unbundling the database asks what changes when views like these take over work the database used to do.

refs.title: Databricks: incremental refresh for materialized views
RisingWave: what is a materialized view
Materialize: views, materialized views and indexes

analogy: A materialized view is the running total a shop keeps on a whiteboard by the till. Recounting every receipt whenever someone asks is the plain query: always right, and slow. Copying last night's recount onto the board is a refresh: quick to read, and wrong by today's sales. Adding each sale as it rings up and subtracting each refund is incremental maintenance: one small step per receipt, and the board stays right. A line for "cheapest item sold today" breaks the trick: when that item is refunded, the board can't say what the next cheapest was without going back through the receipts. The analogy breaks at joins: a whiteboard total depends on one pile of receipts, while a view over a join changes when either side changes, and one renamed merchant can rewrite thousands of its rows.
in_your_world: Settlement and reconciliation reports are where these show up first. A nightly job that rebuilds `daily_merchant_totals` with `TRUNCATE` and `INSERT ... SELECT` is a hand-made materialized view with up to a day of staleness, and its window grows with the ledger. In Oracle the same thing is a materialized view with `REFRESH COMPLETE`, or `REFRESH FAST`, Oracle's incremental refresh, which reads materialized view logs kept on the base tables. In PostgreSQL, refresh with CONCURRENTLY and a unique index so the reports keep answering, or use pg_ivm for small views that must never be stale, and budget the extra time it adds to every ledger write. For dashboards fed from Kafka, a streaming database or a Kafka Streams aggregation keeps the totals current without touching the ledger at all. Whatever you choose, store sums and counts, not averages, and show the reader when the numbers were last refreshed.
mistake: The common mistake is a plain `REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW` on a cron job, against a view that people read all day, run more often each time someone complains about stale numbers. Every plain refresh takes an ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock, so every refresh freezes the dashboard for as long as the query runs; a refresh every minute of a 40-second query leaves it frozen most of the time, while the database recomputes the whole ledger 1,440 times a day. People do it because the first refresh in testing took a second. The fix: add a unique index and refresh CONCURRENTLY so readers never wait, refresh as often as the business needs rather than as often as possible, print the refresh time on the screen, and once the refresh time has grown with the table into minutes, maintain the view incrementally (pg_ivm, or a stream that keeps the totals) instead.

compare.title: The same totals, recomputed on a schedule or maintained by triggers

a.title: a materialized view and a job

compare.note: Both hold the same rows. The first recomputes everything on a schedule and is stale in between; the cost lands on the job, and grows with the table. The second is never stale; the cost lands on every write to payments, and grows with the change. The pg_ivm side wasn't run for this lesson, because the course's PostgreSQL image doesn't include the extension; it follows pg_ivm's README.

worked.title: Maintain a view by hand with delta rules

steps.say: The view keeps count, sum and min per merchant. Start from three merchants.
Insert payment 9 for M-0042, amount 150. Only M-0042's row changes, from the new row alone.
steps.code:
count 3 + 1 = 4
sum   10,450 + 150 = 10,600
min   min(300, 150) = 150
work: 0 base rows read, 1 view row written

steps.say: Delete payment 3, amount 8,900. Above the minimum, so the minimum stays.
steps.code:
count 4 - 1 = 3
sum   10,600 - 8,900 = 1,700
min   8,900 > 150: still 150
work: 0 base rows read, 1 view row written

steps.say: Delete payment 9, amount 150: the minimum. Count and sum are subtractions; the minimum needs M-0042's remaining rows, read through an index on the merchant.
steps.code:
count 3 - 1 = 2
sum   1,700 - 150 = 1,550
min   150 was the min: rescan M-0042 -> 1,250 and 300 -> 300
work: 2 base rows read, 1 view row written

steps.say: The same rules in Kotlin: the lab's `onDelete`. The table has already applied the delete, so `rowsOf` returns the rows that remain.

lab.title: Keep a view up to date with delta rules, and count what it costs
steps: Read the top of `MaterializedView.kt`: `Payment`, the `Inserted` and `Deleted` changes, `Totals` (its average is computed from sum and count), `Work`, and `PaymentTable`, whose `scan` and index lookup `rowsOf` count every row they read. Run the tests once from `labs/`: all 10 fail.

Write `fullRecompute`: one pass over `table.scan(work)`, one `Totals` per merchant, then one view row written per merchant. The first test passes, and the `IncrementalView` constructor, which starts from a full recompute, now works.

Write `onInsert` and `onDelete` in `IncrementalView`. Insert: count + 1, sum + amount, the smaller minimum, or a new row for a new merchant. Delete: count - 1 and sum - amount, remove the row at count 0, and when the deleted amount was the minimum, rescan that merchant with `table.rowsOf` and count a `minRescans`. Eight more tests pass, among them one that checks your view against a full recompute every 100 of 3,000 random changes.
Write `MinTracker`, the other way out: a sorted map from amount to how many rows have it. The last test passes.
Run the Try it's demo again and check its counts against your own reasoning about the 90% batch.
hints: `fullRecompute`: `val out = HashMap<String, Totals>()`; for each payment, `out[p.merchant] = if (t == null) Totals(p.merchant, 1, p.amountCents, p.amountCents) else Totals(...)` with the three updated fields. Add `out.size` to `work.viewRowsWritten` at the end.
Count `work.viewRowsWritten++` exactly once per change in both functions, whether the row is created, updated or removed. The cost tests count on it.

`onDelete` runs after the table applied the delete, like an AFTER trigger, so `table.rowsOf(p.merchant, work)` returns the remaining rows; take `minOf { it.amountCents }`. Check `t.count == 1L` first: an empty group has no minimum to find.

`MinTracker`: `counts.merge(v, 1, Int::plus)` to add; to remove, `counts[v] ?: throw IllegalArgumentException(...)`, then `counts.remove(v)` when the count is 1, else store count - 1. `min` is `counts.firstKey()` when the map isn't empty.

drill.title: Delta rules from memory
drill.prompt: Without looking: write the delta rules for a view with count, sum, avg and min per group, for an insert of a value x and for a delete of x. Say which case needs the base table and the two ways around it. Then say how many grouping sets `GROUP BY CUBE (a, b, c, d)` produces.

answer.src:
insert x into group g             delete x from group g
  count += 1                        count -= 1     (0: remove g's row)
  sum   += x                        sum   -= x
  min    = min(min, x)              x > min: min unchanged
  avg    = sum / count, on read     x == min: the next min isn't in the view
                                      1. rescan g in the base table (needs an index on g)
                                      2. or keep a sorted multiset of values per group (memory)

CUBE (a, b, c, d): 2^4 = 16 grouping sets, from (a, b, c, d) down to ()

recap: A materialized view stores a query's result as a table, plus a rule for keeping it right. Like an index, it makes some reads cheap and costs work whenever the data changes.

`REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW` reruns the whole query: its cost follows the data, not the change, and the view is stale between refreshes. A plain refresh blocks readers with an ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock; CONCURRENTLY needs a unique index, lets reads continue, and does more work.

Incremental view maintenance applies delta rules: count and sum add and subtract, average is sum over count, min and max need the base table or extra state when the extreme value is deleted, and joins need the other table's matching rows.
Deltas win when changes are few; a batch that rewrites most of the data is cheaper to recompute, which is why Snowflake has an ADAPTIVE mode.
A data cube is a stored GROUP BY CUBE: all 2^n grouping sets of its dimensions. It answers grouped questions about those dimensions from a few rows and nothing else, so the raw data stays.

pg_ivm maintains views with triggers in the same transaction; Snowflake dynamic tables and Databricks materialized views refresh on a schedule, incrementally when they can; Materialize and RisingWave keep views current from streams of changes.

quiz.q: A view keeps per-merchant count, sum and average of payment amounts, maintained incrementally. Which of them should it actually store?
options: All three, so reads need no arithmetic
Count and sum; the average is sum / count when read
Only the average, the number the dashboard shows
Sum and average; count can be derived as sum / average
quiz.why: Count and sum each have a delta rule: an insert adds, a delete subtracts. An average has none: taking one payment out of it needs the count anyway, and storing it next to count and sum gives two copies that can disagree. Deriving count as sum / average fails as soon as the average is 0 and is never exact with rounding.

quiz.q: A dashboard reads a materialized view whose query takes 15 minutes. During each hourly plain REFRESH, the dashboard hangs. What does switching to `REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW CONCURRENTLY` change?
options: The refresh takes about a minute, because it only reads the changed rows
Nothing, unless the view is also made UNLOGGED
Readers keep reading the old contents while it runs, and the refresh takes at least as long, because it reruns the query and then compares old and new
The view becomes incrementally maintained between refreshes
quiz.why: CONCURRENTLY swaps the ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock for an EXCLUSIVE one that lets SELECTs run, and applies only the differences to the view. But it still runs the whole 15-minute query first and then diffs the result against the old contents, so it costs more work, not less. Making the work follow the change needs incremental maintenance.

quiz.q: From lesson 7: a view maintained incrementally is `SELECT ... FROM payments JOIN merchants ON m.id = p.merchant_id`. Each inserted payment must be joined to its merchant. What keeps that delta cheap?
options: An index on `merchants.id`, so each delta is one index lookup instead of a scan of merchants
A bigger `work_mem`, so the join runs in memory
A unique index on the view
Nothing: a delta never reads other tables
quiz.why: The delta of a join for a new payment is that payment joined with the merchants table, so the maintenance reads the other side once per changed row. With lesson 7's B+tree on the join key that's a few page reads; without it, each insert scans merchants and the incremental path can cost more than a full refresh. A unique index on the view is what CONCURRENTLY needs, a different thing.

quiz.q: A view maintains `min(amount)` per merchant incrementally, with no extra state. Which change forces it to read the base table?
options: Inserting a payment smaller than the current minimum
Inserting the first payment of a new merchant
Deleting a payment above the merchant's minimum
Deleting the payment that holds the merchant's minimum, while the merchant has other payments
quiz.why: Inserts only compare with the stored minimum, and a new merchant starts its row from the one payment. Deleting a larger amount can't change the minimum. Deleting the minimum itself leaves the view without the next smallest value, which only the base table (or a per-group sorted multiset) has. If it was the merchant's last payment, the row is simply removed.

quiz.q: A materialized view stores `GROUP BY CUBE (day, currency, category)` with count and sum over payments. Which question can it not answer?
options: Total SEK payments on 5 October, across all categories
The share of the money that came from payments over 500 euros
The number of payments per category over all days
The grand total
quiz.why: A cube answers questions about its dimensions: each of the other three is one cell at some level of the cube. The amount of each payment isn't a dimension; the cube summed the amounts into cells and kept nothing about single payments, so a threshold on them needs the raw rows. That's why warehouses keep the detail and use cubes as accelerators.

flashcards.back: A query's result stored as a table, which can be indexed and read like one, plus a rule for refreshing it. Reads are cheap; it is stale between refreshes.

flashcards.front: What does `REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW CONCURRENTLY` need, and what does it buy?
flashcards.back: A unique index on plain columns covering every row. Readers keep reading (EXCLUSIVE lock instead of ACCESS EXCLUSIVE); the refresh does more work, not less.

flashcards.front: Delta rules for COUNT and SUM?
flashcards.back: Insert x: count + 1, sum + x. Delete x: count - 1, sum - x, and remove the group's row at count 0.

flashcards.front: Why is MIN hard to maintain incrementally?
flashcards.back: When the deleted row was the minimum, the next smallest value isn't in the view. Rescan the group through an index (pg_ivm) or keep a sorted multiset per group (streaming engines).

flashcards.front: How many grouping sets does `GROUP BY CUBE` over n columns produce?
flashcards.back: 2^n: every subset of the columns, down to () for the grand total.

flashcards.front: When is incremental refresh slower than a full one?
flashcards.back: When a large share of the data changed: per-row deltas (and MIN rescans) add up past one pass over the table. Snowflake's ADAPTIVE mode rebuilds in that case.

flashcards.front: What does Snowflake's AUTO refresh mode do?
flashcards.back: Picks INCREMENTAL or FULL once, when the dynamic table is created, and never re-evaluates, so set the mode yourself for production tables.

terms.plain: A stored query result that can be indexed and read like a table, refreshed by recomputing or by applying changes.
How far a materialized view is behind its base tables; between refreshes readers see old answers.
Updating a materialized view by applying the changes to its inputs instead of recomputing it.
The rule that turns a change to an input, such as an inserted or deleted row, into a change to the view.
Aggregates precomputed for every combination of a set of dimensions, with totals along each one.
One way of grouping inside a GROUP BY; CUBE lists all 2^n of them for n columns.
In Snowflake, how far behind its sources a dynamic table may fall before it is refreshed.

explain_back.prompt: A product owner asks why the merchant dashboard's totals can be 10 minutes old, and why we don't simply refresh the view every second. Explain what a refresh costs, what incremental maintenance changes, and what you would propose.
explain_back.answer: The dashboard reads a materialized view: the totals were computed once and stored, so each page load reads a few rows instead of recounting a million payments. The catch is that a refresh reruns the whole query. It reads every payment, even if only one changed, so its cost grows with the ledger, and a plain refresh also locks the view so the dashboard waits while it runs. Refreshing every second would mean recomputing the whole ledger 86,400 times a day. Incremental maintenance flips that around: instead of recomputing, it applies each change as a delta, adding a new payment to its merchant's count and sum and subtracting a refund, so the work follows the change, not the data. It has hard cases: minimums when the smallest payment is deleted, joins that need the other table, and big batches, where recomputing is cheaper. I'd propose moving the dashboard's totals to incremental maintenance, with pg_ivm if it stays inside PostgreSQL or a streaming view fed from our payments topic if it doesn't, keep counts and sums rather than averages, and show the last-updated time on the screen either way.

deeper.body:
**Duplicates and DISTINCT.** A view with DISTINCT can't delete a row just because one source row went away: another source row may produce the same result. Maintained views keep a count per result row instead, pg_ivm in a hidden `__ivm_count__` column, and remove the row only when the count reaches zero. The same counting is what makes deltas through projections and unions correct.

**Deltas of deltas.** The delta of a query is itself a query, over the changed rows and the old state. Research systems took that further: maintain the delta queries incrementally too, so that even a join's delta is answered from small maintained state. Materialize grew out of the Timely and Differential Dataflow research projects, which build every operator, joins and aggregates included, so that it consumes and produces changes rather than whole tables.

**Query rewrite.** Oracle can answer a query from a materialized view the query never names: its optimizer notices that `SELECT sum(amount) FROM payments WHERE day = ...` can be computed from a matching summary view and rewrites the plan. PostgreSQL doesn't; a query uses a materialized view only if it names it. Warehouses that keep many cubes rely on this kind of rewrite so that analysts can query the raw tables and still hit the summaries.

**Freshness has to be visible.** A materialized view that is 10 minutes behind looks exactly like one that is current. Store the refresh time in the view or next to it, and show it wherever the numbers are shown.
